To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

portal‐systemic (portacaval) shunting of rats for 3,8 and 16weeks was associated with a progressive fall in the brain glucose content and that this was accompanied by an increase in the brain glucose‐6‐phosphatase and fructose‐diphosphate contents, which may be a tentative mechanism of sensitizing the brain in liver disease.
The effect of portocaval shunting (PCS) on brain glycogen and glucose content and on brain glycolysis and the citric acid cycle was investigated in rats after 3, 6 and 16 weeks of PCS.
portal‐systemic anastomosis causes a progressive fall in glucose and changes in brain glycolytic intermediates which may contribute to brain metabolic perturbation in hepatic encephalopathy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of portacausal shunting on the brain metabolism.
the effect of sustained portal‐venous to systemic shunting on brain metabolism.
the effect of portal-systemic shunting on brain energy metabolism.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

portal‐systemic diversion in the rat is accompanied by a progressive decrease in brain glucose, a decrease in the glycolytic intermediate fructose‐1‐6‐diphosphatase and an increase in glucose‐6‐phosphatase and fructose‐6‐phospate.
the metabolic effects of PC shunting on brain glucose and glycolytic and tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediates are not as dramatic as might have been expected from previous studies.

portacaval shunting in the rat is accompanied by a progressive decrease in brain glucose content, a reduction in brain glycogen content and changes in the glycolytic and Krebs cycle intermediates which could indicate an increased flux through the glycolytic pathway and a decreased flux through the Krebs cycle.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the effect of portacavel shunting on the brain was a decrease in glucose and an increase in the citric‐acid‐cycle intermediates, with a concomitant increase in the glycolytic intermediate glucose‐6‐phophate and a decrease in the glycolysis end product fructose‐1‐6‐diphophate.
PC shunting in the rat is accompanied by an increase of brain lactate which is due to a fall in brain glucose and to a change in the balance of glycolytic intermediates.
the brain of portacaval shunted rats has a reduced glucose supply, an increased glycolytic capacity but a reduced glycolytic flux.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain can be sensitized in liver disease by the combination of reduced glucose availability and inhibition of glycolysis.
the effect of portacavalligation on brain glycogen was not significant.
the brain in liver disease may have a different metabolic profile to normal brain.
